title: Human-Backed Login for Senior-Serving Software
one_liner: A drop-in login layer for apps whose users are 65+ that replaces passwords with a two-tap flow, a spoken one-time code by phone call (landline included), family delegates and a live concierge who can walk anyone in.
customer: Vertical SaaS vendors whose users are older adults: senior-living and home-care family portals, community and church software, benefits and Medicare-broker portals, pharmacy and telehealth apps, funeral-planning tools. They pay about $0.80-2 per active senior per month, $3 per concierge-assisted login, with a $299/month minimum.
problem: An operator of a ~10-year-old SaaS used heavily by people 65+ says users 'are tired and frustrated about remembering the domain/path to login screen and then which email/password they used', and that simplification has not fixed it. The 60 responses show what fails: forced resets, masked passwords, magic links (older users struggle switching apps), QR codes and passkeys. What people say they'd pay for is a human: 'elderly individuals want a solution rather than a lesson', and a 'code that you can type in on another device... my grandmother could call and read me a code'.
solution: Per-customer short vanity login URL plus a large 'Call me' button that triggers a phone call reading a short code aloud, working for landlines and flip phones, then persistent trusted-device sessions that effectively never log out. A family-delegate approve/reset flow, no forced password rotation, and no masked fields by default. When automation fails, a live concierge line verifies identity via vendor-supplied challenge questions and completes recovery. Ship as an SDK/widget plus hosted pages, with audit logs suitable for HIPAA-adjacent customers, and report the reduction in login-related support tickets per customer.
why_now: Big platforms pushed passkeys to consumers in 2025-2026 and older users, and the relatives who support them, are loudly reporting confusion and lockouts. The same vendors are under pressure to support MFA. Telephony APIs make voice-delivered codes cheap, and support cost per senior user is the metric operators feel.
revenue_model: Per-active-senior monthly fee, per-assisted-login fee for concierge calls, $299/month minimum, and an annual contract with an ticket-reduction guarantee for larger vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Authentication products optimize against attackers; for the 65+ user the dominant failure is support cost and churn, and the operators in the thread say the answer they would pay for is a human plus a code they can read out loud, not a better protocol. Every fashionable option (passkeys, magic links, QR) was named as failing for this group in the same thread. Evidence: Ask HN 'Easiest UX for Seniors', 58 points, 60 comments https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47729327; passkey confusion for elderly relatives and recovery gaps https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49010448.
first_30_days: Wire Twilio Verify's voice channel to a hosted 'Call me to log in' page and staff a three-person phone shift. Pitch 20 founders of senior-vertical SaaS (found via LinkedIn and association vendor directories), starting with the Ask HN author. Offer a $299/month 60-day pilot that measures login-related support tickets before and after, and convert on a shown reduction.

title: Harvest Inns: Motel Wings as Farm Crew Housing
one_liner: A hospitality-grade operator that master-leases wings of underused rural motels and sublets compliant beds, meals and transport to growers who cannot house H-2A crews.
customer: Fruit and vegetable growers and grower associations using H-2A labor in Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Washington and Florida. The supply side is independent rural motels and extended-stay properties.
problem: Housing is the binding constraint on legally staffing harvests. Farm crews shrank after the immigration crackdown (up to 30% of strawberry and almond crews lost in Q1 2026), grapes, blueberries and peaches rotted unpicked in 2025, and H-2A jobs are heading toward 500K. Growers do not want to run hotels, and motel owners do not want H-2A paperwork while their occupancy stays weak in a K-shaped market.
solution: Master-lease 20-40 room wings for 10-16 weeks. Run the compliance layer: DOL public-accommodation rules (50 sq ft per person, 36-inch bed spacing, cooking and laundry ratios, direct payment by the employer to housing management), pre-built state workforce agency inspection files, linens and cleaning, catered or kitchenette meals and van shuttles. Software rebooks the same crews' beds in the next county as harvest calendars move, like a hotel chain whose guests are harvest crews. Inspection-first and worker-first standards are the moat.
why_now: DOL rules explicitly allow hotels and motels as H-2A housing, with local health codes applying first. The October 2025 wage-rule change and H-2A growth mean more growers are entering a system they have never staffed. Late crews and unpicked fields are now widely reported, and lower-tier hotels are under pressure while luxury leads.
revenue_model: Growers pay roughly $22-$35 per bed-night all-in (assumption to validate), of which motels get about $12-$20. Operator margin of 20-30% plus meal and transport upsells, sold as season contracts through grower associations.
non_obvious_insight: The idle asset already exists in every farm county, and the missing party is a specialist workforce-lodging operator, the ag version of oil-field man camps, who will absorb compliance risk. Motel owners value a guaranteed off-OTA base load more than a higher rate.
first_30_days: Pick one cluster such as south Georgia blueberries and peaches or Michigan cherries. Sign 3 motels for wings of 20-40 rooms, map the state inspection process with the workforce agency, and pre-sell 2 growers before March for the spring 2027 harvest season.

title: Courthouse Tape: Land-Assembly Radar for Infrastructure
one_liner: A daily feed that reads recorded option memoranda, leases and easements to show who is quietly assembling land for data centers, solar and transmission weeks before anyone announces it.
customer: Competing data center, solar, storage and transmission developers' land teams and site-selection consultants; utility and co-op large-load planners; infrastructure and energy funds buying alternative data; and county economic development and planning offices wanting defensive visibility.
problem: Land assembly is a race, and the first public trace is a short memorandum of option, lease or easement recorded at the county. Nobody watches those at scale. The assessor doesn't reflect an unexercised option. The clerk's document-type field is a dropdown chosen by a data-entry clerk, so big deals hide under 'Other', 'Miscellaneous' or 'Agreement'. Developers find out about a competitor's 6,000 acres months late, counties learn from a leaked newspaper story, and everyone pays landmen $300-$600 a day to sit in vaults.
solution: Ingest recorded instruments from county portals and bulk feeds in target corridors. Classify by reading the full image, not the clerk's label. Cluster by grantee, signatory, notary, return-to law firm and mailing address to unmask LLC families. Flag assembly events, such as N option memos within X miles or easement clusters along a line that imply transmission or pipeline. Deliver alerts, a map, and parcel-level chain-of-title and existing-easement packets on demand, with a human landman reviewing the hard ones.
why_now: The 2025-2026 large-load land rush is real: options in Hallam, Nebraska are reportedly worth tens of thousands of dollars an acre, and Hill County, Texas land appraised near $7,100 an acre has been offered about $100,000 an acre. Options are documented only by memoranda under NDA. FinCEN's 2025 decision to exempt domestic companies from beneficial-ownership reporting means LLC unmasking has to come from primary records. LLM vision finally reads messy scanned instruments accurately.
revenue_model: $2k-$8k/month per regional developer or utility seat, $750-$2,000 per tract title packet, and $50k-$150k/year alt-data licenses for funds. Optional revenue share or free access for counties that provide bulk feeds.
non_obvious_insight: The return-to address and notary on a recorded memorandum are the fingerprint of the developer's counsel, and they reveal an assembly weeks before a rezoning hearing. The mislabeled document-type field is why nobody has done this with generic data vendors. Landmen are the recorder's best regulars and know exactly which counties are hot, which makes them the cheapest ground-truth labelers and first customers.
first_30_days: Choose two counties with a rumored project, pull 24 months of instruments, and build the classifier and clustering. Deliver a 'who is assembling where' memo free to 10 site-selection consultants and land brokers, then convert two into $3k-$5k pilots. Check each state's bulk-data commercial-use rules and offer the counties access to the same maps.

title: Special-Tool Exchange for Retiring Regional Fleets
one_liner: Buy or take on consignment the OEM special tooling stranded when regionals retire 50-seat jets and older turboprops, calibrate it, and rent or sell it to operators who cannot get it from the OEM for months.
customer: MROs and Part 145 shops adding a regional-jet or turboprop type, Part 135 and cargo operators, freighter-conversion programs, and operators in Latin America, Africa and Asia flying older regional types. Sellers are regional airlines and lessors with tooling cages to empty.
problem: Every type needs OEM special tooling: rigging pins, wing and gear jack adapters, engine sling adapters, pinning tools, pressure-test rigs, borescope adapters, prop and control-rigging fixtures. New from the OEM this is expensive and lead times can run to months, and some tooling is out of production. When a regional retires a subfleet, that tooling is on the tool-control ledger at near-zero book value, taking up cage space. It gets scrapped, shipped out with airframes, or forgotten. Buyers who are desperate for it have no idea the seller exists, and vice versa.
solution: A consignment marketplace and rental pool. Take tooling in from retiring fleets at no cash outlay, on a 70/30 split of sales and rentals. Inspect it, get it recalibrated through a metrology lab, tag it with a certificate, and catalog it with photos and drawing references. Rent it weekly or monthly with a deposit and freight, or sell it. Offer starter tooling bundles for a shop taking on a new type, such as everything needed for a first C-check on that airframe.
why_now: Majors keep replacing 50-seat regional jets and older turboprops with larger regional aircraft, so tooling cages empty every quarter. Cargo conversions and second-life operators in emerging markets are keeping the old types flying. OEM lead times and parts availability have been poor across the industry since 2022, so buyers will pay to skip the wait.
revenue_model: Consignment split on sales, rental fees at roughly 3-6% of replacement value per month, calibration and freight margin, and bundle pricing for new-type start-ups. Later, a subscription for shops that want guaranteed access to a tooling pool.
non_obvious_insight: Tooling has none of the obsolescence problem of parts. It does not expire except for calibration. A directors of maintenance would rather give it away than pay to store it, and nobody knows who the buyers are. The unusual thing about this business is that the inventory is almost free and the demand is urgent, because a missing pin can ground an airplane for weeks.
first_30_days: Call 20 directors of maintenance, tech-services managers and lessor technical reps whose subfleets are winding down. Get two or three tool cages on consignment with no upfront cash. Photograph and catalog them, send calibrated items to a local metrology lab, and publish a simple catalog with rental terms and a deposit process. Contact freighter-conversion programs, Part 135 operators and international MROs that fly the same type. The first rental should close within weeks, because the urgency price is high.

title: Used-Satellite Exchange With Independent Health Reports
one_liner: A broker and due-diligence shop that turns dead or distressed operators' on-orbit assets into sellable, verified inventory.
customer: Buyers: acquirers of the Rocket Lab type, infrastructure and PE funds, and governments or startups that want a quick constellation. Sellers: bankruptcy trustees, venture-debt lenders, insurers and cash-strapped first-generation smallsat operators.
problem: Insiders assume a satellite is worthless when its company dies. But the bus, license, orbit and customer contracts can still hold value, and buyers cannot verify condition. Lenders have no repossession or title process, and every M&A team improvises technical diligence.
solution: Two products. (1) An independent 'fleet health report' built from open orbital data (maneuver history, decay, propulsion-use proxies, beacon and telemetry checks) plus data-room review. (2) A brokerage that matches on-orbit assets and licenses to buyers, with regulator-approved license transfers handled by counsel.
why_now: Rocket Lab's roughly $8B Iridium deal and its CFO's 'more M&A' comment show on-orbit assets are being priced. 4,517 satellites deployed in 2025 means a large aging first-generation cohort. Funding is bifurcating into nine-figure rounds for a few winners and starvation for the rest.
revenue_model: $25-100k per health report. 3-8% success fee on brokered deals. Annual subscription for lenders and insurers who want portfolio monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: In space, value sits in the license, the orbit and the operating bus, and none of the three dies with the company. The missing piece is trusted third-party verification, which is a service business rather than a rocket business.
first_30_days: Publish free health scorecards on 20 public constellations to build credibility. Interview five venture-debt lenders and two space insurers about their current diligence. Sell two paid reports to funds looking at consolidation targets. Ask trustees of failed smallsat companies to list assets with you.

title: Whey Capture Skids for Small Cheesemakers
one_liner: Leased containerized filtration skids that turn small cheese plants' cheap whey into sellable protein concentrate.
customer: Regional and farmstead cheese plants that sell whey for pennies or pay to dispose of it.
problem: Whey protein is scarce and pricey, yet small plants lack the ultrafiltration equipment and offtake to capture it, because equipment makers sell to giants.
solution: A leased, containerized ultrafiltration and diafiltration skid on revenue share, producing liquid whey protein concentrate that we sell to partner dryers and beverage makers.
why_now: Whey concentrate is up 108% in two years and isolate reaches $14/lb, so the byproduct now outearns its economics at small scale.
revenue_model: Skid lease plus a 30-40% revenue share on concentrate sold.
non_obvious_insight: The byproduct ate the product, and the largest untapped upside sits with small plants that big equipment vendors ignore.
first_30_days: Tour five plants in WI, VT and CA, quote a used UF skid, and pre-sell offtake to one beverage brand and one dryer.

title: Fractional Operator for Tiny Private Water Systems
one_liner: A flat-fee compliance back office and operator-of-record for the mobile-home parks, small subdivisions and rural employers that own small water systems and are about to face PFAS testing in 2027.
customer: Owners of mobile-home parks, small private water companies and HOA systems, and rural employers or private schools with their own wells. These are community and non-transient non-community systems, typically under 3,300 people. The owner is often an aging individual or family LLC with no operations staff.
problem: Owners face initial PFAS monitoring in 2027 and a 4.0 ppt limit still on the books. EPA's May 2026 proposal would move compliance from 2029 to 2031 and drop limits on four other compounds. The lead action level tightens on Nov 1, 2027. The whiplash freezes capex. Nobody at the business knows the sampling calendar, the accredited lab, the state portal, or the money ($1B of IIJA earmarked for PFAS testing and treatment, $7.2B of FY2026 SRF). The owner also cannot sell, because a first sample becomes a disclosure.
solution: Wedge: a $1,500 flat 'PFAS-2027 Readiness Pack' covering the sampling plan, lab coordination, result interpretation against 4.0 ppt, state filing and an options memo (treat, interconnect, drill, or sell). Upsell to a $600/mo retainer for the sampling calendar, consumer confidence report, lead inventory, monthly operator logs, tenant submetered billing and bookkeeping for a segregated water fund. The operator-of-record role is subcontracted to a state-certified operator partner. Later, broker and operate systems whose owners want out.
why_now: EPA's May 2026 proposals to delay PFAS compliance and rescind four limits have left small owners paralyzed, while 2027 initial monitoring still stands. Public money is earmarked: $1B IIJA for PFAS, $7.2B FY2026 SRF, and states are pushing consolidation of non-viable systems. The Boomer ownership wave is hitting the same long tail of tiny systems. EPA's science office was eliminated in 2026, so owners get less federal guidance.
revenue_model: $1,500 Readiness Pack. $400-$900/mo retainer per system by size. 6% success fee on SRF or state grants won. 2-4% brokerage fee on systems sold, plus an option to acquire orphan systems at distressed multiples using consolidation money.
non_obvious_insight: Federal delay does not remove the liability that appears at the first sample. Once a 2027 result exists it becomes a disclosure item in any sale, loan or insurance renewal. So the smart small owner samples early and under a plan. The firm that holds the compliance record becomes the natural buyer of last resort for a long tail of systems too small for the big acquirers. The retainer is the cheapest way to source those succession deals.
first_30_days: Sign one retired state-certified operator as partner and one accredited PFAS lab for a bulk rate. Join two state manufactured-housing associations and the state rural water association. Run free 'is my system covered?' webinars. Sell 10 Readiness Packs at $1,500 in one state, and use the results to prep 3 grant applications. Start compliance-only and add operator-of-record after the partner clears state rules.

title: 30-Day Capacity-Window Plan After Early Alzheimer's Diagnosis
one_liner: A productized sprint that uses the legally competent window after an early blood-test diagnosis to lock down legal, financial, safety and care plans.
customer: Newly diagnosed patients and their spouses or adult children, reached through memory clinics, neurology and primary-care practices, blood-test labs and elder-law firms. Employers with caregiver benefits are a secondary buyer.
problem: Blood tests cleared in 2025 mean many people learn they're on the path to dementia while still competent, with a 3-7 year window to sign POAs, choose agents, set financial guardrails, plan driving and firearm safety, decide on Leqembi and record wishes. After capacity is lost, it becomes a court fight. CMS GUIDE closed enrollment after one 2024 window, so nobody owns the first 30 days.
solution: A fixed-fee, nurse-navigator-led sprint: a capacity-timed legal package via partner attorneys (POAs, directives, HIPAA releases, updated will or trust), financial guardrails (bill-pay automation, bank trusted-contact, scam locks), a safety plan (driving, firearms, stove, wandering), a care roadmap with cost projections and a Leqembi decision aid, and 90 days of dyad coaching.
why_now: FDA cleared Lumipulse pTau217 in May 2025 and a second primary-care blood test in Oct 2025. Leqembi Q1 sales rose 74% to $168M and it now has an at-home subcutaneous starting dose. Diagnosis is decentralizing while post-diagnosis coordination is not.
revenue_model: $1,500-3,500 fixed family fee, plus employer or LTC-insurer contracts. No referral payments from providers, to stay clear of anti-kickback issues.
non_obvious_insight: Earlier diagnosis is a legal-capacity clock, not just a medical event. The valuable window is the one when the patient can still sign, and every document signed in it prevents a $5-15k guardianship later.
first_30_days: Partner with two memory clinics and three elder-law firms, and deliver five pilot sprints at $1,500 each. Track documents executed while competent and family satisfaction.

title: Youth Clubs as the Ban-Proof Group Chat
one_liner: A roster-anchored messaging layer for sports leagues, scout councils and youth groups that reuses the club's adult-verified roster as a safe, auditable chat for 9-15 year olds, paid by the club.
customer: Regional youth sports leagues, scout councils, robotics/FIRST teams and church youth groups (5k-100k members), plus their liability insurers. Parents use it free.
problem: Under-16 bans (Australia, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, several US states) push kids into private chats and games. Everyone's answer is a new 'safe social network for kids', which dies on cold start. Meanwhile clubs already hold the verified network (background-checked coaches, rosters, parent contacts) but run it on WhatsApp, GroupMe and Snap groups with coach-to-child DMs. Youth-safety policies such as SafeSport's (from memory) prohibit exactly those DMs, and leagues cannot audit them.
solution: Team and league chats built on the registration data the club already has (DOB, parent identity). No one-to-one adult-minor DMs unless a second guardian is copied. Kid accounts are age-tiered and parent-linked, with no discovery, ads or strangers. Keyword flags go to the club safety officer. An exportable audit log goes to the insurer. Kids age out into open platforms at 16.
why_now: Ban leakage (VPNs under A$20 a month, 75% of Australian teens planning to stay on) means kids need somewhere else to talk. Insurers are tightening abuse-and-molestation coverage (from memory). Fall registration season is happening now, so the product can ride the season's registration fee.
revenue_model: $1-4 per member per season, bundled into the league's registration fee. Enterprise licence for councils. Referral fees or premium credits from insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The hard part of safe kids' social is distribution and verification, not software. A club has the graph, the identity check, a legal duty of care and a budget, and nobody has packaged that.
first_30_days: Interview 15 league directors and two youth-sports insurers. Ship a white-label chat on Stream or Sendbird for two leagues in one metro. Sell it as 'audit-ready coach-athlete messaging' at $1 per kid during fall registration. Collect an insurer endorsement or premium-credit letter.

title: Walkable Childhood Homes for Memory Care
one_liner: Generate explorable 3D versions of a person's childhood street, lost home or homeland from a few photos and stories, delivered on a TV or tablet for memory care, hospice and diaspora families.
customer: Memory-care and assisted-living communities (activity budgets), hospices and adult children, paying $250-600 per scene or $300-600 a month per community.
problem: Reminiscence is among the best-supported non-drug interventions for dementia and late-life low mood, but the props are still photos and music. Existing VR programs offer generic 'visit Paris' content, not personal places. Immigrants, refugees and the bereaved have no visual way back to a home that no longer exists.
solution: A studio workflow: family interview intake, photo and archival-map collection, a world-model pipeline that builds an era-appropriate walkable scene, and a docent mode where staff or grandchildren ask 'what was on this corner?'. Human artists finalize each scene to remove uncanny or distressing artifacts, and a gentle mode limits sensory intensity.
why_now: Generative world models released in 2025 (Google's Genie 3, World Labs' Marble and similar) can create persistent, explorable scenes from a handful of images. That cuts the cost of a personalized environment from thousands of dollars to well under $100 of compute.
revenue_model: Per-scene fees, community subscriptions for scene libraries and refreshes, hospice partnerships, and a consumer gift channel for diaspora families.
non_obvious_insight: Reminiscence works best when it is specific and shared, and personalization used to cost too much. The most valuable scenes are not beautiful cities but the ordinary corner, kitchen and street a person actually lived on.
first_30_days: Offer 10 memory-care communities three free scenes each, generated from residents' family photos. Track engagement and agitation logs with staff, then sell five-scene packs at $500 and add one hospice partner.

title: Voucher Lease-Up Desk for Soft Markets
one_liner: An ops service that gets units voucher-ready and through housing-authority inspection and paperwork in days, turning Section 8 from a hassle into the cheapest demand source in a soft market.
customer: Mid-size multifamily operators (300-5,000 units) in soft Sun Belt markets with high concessions, with housing authorities and mobility nonprofits as secondary payers.
problem: Apartment List shows 7.0% vacancy, 34 days to lease (longest September since 2019) and concessions on 15.8% of stabilized units (Austin 37%). Yet many operators still avoid Housing Choice Voucher applicants because inspection scheduling and contract paperwork can stretch weeks, costing roughly $300+ of rent a week on a $1,388 median unit. Voucher holders, meanwhile, fail to find units.
solution: A virtual pre-inspection app that walks site staff through HUD's NSPIRE-based checklist with photos so units pass first time. It automates the tenancy-approval and contract packet and tracks status across 50-100 local housing authorities, checks rent-reasonableness and payment standards before pricing, and publishes a live 'voucher-ready units' feed to caseworkers.
why_now: Time-to-lease is at a multi-year high and concessions are replacing rent growth, so landlords will trade a small admin burden for near-guaranteed rent. Authority inspections have moved to one federal standard, which a checklist app can encode.
revenue_model: $350-600 per successful voucher lease-up (against a $1,400 month of vacancy) or $1.50 per unit per month subscription, plus contracts with authorities and mobility programs.
non_obvious_insight: Operators treat vouchers as a risk problem when it is a cycle-time problem, measured in days, which is exactly what a 34-day-to-lease market prices. Government pays most of the rent, so the lowest-CAC tenant class is being left on the table. Housing-authority funding stress is the main risk, so sell to authorities with reserves and use source-of-income laws as a second wedge.
first_30_days: Pick two metros. Call 20 regional managers and offer a free pre-inspection pilot on 10 vacant units. Partner with two authority landlord-liaison offices and one mobility nonprofit. Charge only per lease-up once the unit is under contract with the authority.

title: Universal Viva: AI-Run Oral Verification
one_liner: After each major submission the student takes a five-minute identity-verified voice conversation with an AI examiner about their own work, and humans review only the flagged mismatches.
customer: Online and community-college programs, university departments, dual-enrollment providers and credentialing bootcamps (department chairs and deans), later honor councils.
problem: At Harvard 89% of professors received suspected AI work but only 12% referred cases, and 67% say AI hurts their courses. Detectors are unreliable and biased against non-native writers (lower-confidence data). Oral exams work but do not scale: 300 students at 15 minutes each is 75 hours.
solution: A voice agent reads the submission, asks 6-8 adaptive questions on reasoning, sources and choices, checks consistency with the submitted work, and returns a comprehension score. Low-scoring cases go to a bench of trained human examiners. It measures whether the student understands the work rather than accusing anyone of using AI, with accommodations for disabilities and language.
why_now: Real-time voice models with natural turn-taking and low latency matured in 2025-26. Faculty sentiment has turned sharply negative and detection has failed, so institutions need a fairer alternative before the next term's grades.
revenue_model: $3-6 per verification paid by the institution or $30 per student per course, with premium pricing for human audit and site licenses.
non_obvious_insight: Detection asks 'did an AI write this?', which is unanswerable and adversarial. Verification asks 'does the student understand this?', which is answerable, fairer to non-native writers, and much harder to outsource live in a voice conversation.
first_30_days: Pilot with 3 professors in writing-intensive intro courses at a community college, about 60 students. Compare oral-comprehension scores with graded essays and show an instructor dashboard. Move to $4 per verification after the pilot. Set voice-data retention and accessibility policies before launch.

title: Wet-Lab Materials Bill-of-Materials Scanner
one_liner: Black Duck for biology: scan a startup's plasmids, cell lines, antibodies and enzymes for license, MTA and patent encumbrances before an investor or acquirer does.
customer: Venture-backed biotechs 6-12 months from a Series B, IPO or M&A, acquirers' diligence teams, university spinouts, and IP counsel.
problem: Materials used freely in academia carry limits in for-profit use: Addgene third-party limited-use label licenses, research-only cell-line licenses, Cas9, base-editor and promoter patents, and MTA restrictions. Nobody inventories a lab's biological dependencies, so surprises surface in diligence and cut price or delay closing. At least 12 funded biotechs were sold for $1B+ in 2026, so acquirer diligence is intense.
solution: Ingest LIMS or Benchling exports, plasmid GenBank files and strain and cell-line lists. Match them against a curated encumbrance database (Addgene label-license data, depositor MTAs, patent sequence claims, vendor terms). Output a risk-ranked report with remediation options (license, replace, design around), continuous scanning as inventory changes, and attorney-reviewed summaries.
why_now: Deal volume is high, LIMS exports are easy, and software license scanning is a well-understood category that buyers already recognize.
revenue_model: $12-40k per scan, $30-100k annual continuous monitoring, and sprint pricing for acquirers' diligence teams.
non_obvious_insight: In software, license scanning is standard. In biology the dependencies are physical, unlisted and cross borders, so no bill of materials exists. One database sells to both sides: acquirers use it to find hidden liabilities, startups use it to fix them cheaply before the deal.
first_30_days: Build scanner v0 for plasmid sequences against about 200 known encumbered parts and labels. Run free scans for 10 startups through the SynBioBeta network and convert 3 to $12-15k audits. Recruit an IP attorney as advisor.

title: Pharma Load Attribution for EU Producer-Pays Wastewater
one_liner: A neutral, audit-grade dataset showing which drugs from which producers, in which aging catchments and care homes, create the micropollutant load that EU pharma companies must now pay at least 80% of treatment for.
customer: National extended-producer-responsibility scheme operators and pharma/cosmetics trade bodies. Regional water boards and utilities deciding which large plants get quaternary treatment first also buy. Pricing is EUR 25-80k per study and EUR 100-250k a year for licenses.
problem: The recast Urban Wastewater Directive makes pharma and cosmetics producers fund at least 80% of quaternary treatment. The payment scheme is due by end-2028, and 20% of large plants must be upgraded by 2033. Annual cost estimates differ about 10x (EC EUR 1.2B, JRC EUR 1.56B, EurEau EUR 3.6-11.2B, Spain alone EUR 24.5B), and nobody owns the attribution of kilograms of active ingredient to payers. Older adults, care homes and hospitals are the concentrated source of medication residues, and Europe's 80+ cohort is its fastest-growing.
solution: A catchment-level model combining national dispensing statistics by age band, care-home and hospital bed registers, excretion and plant-removal rates, and receiving-water flow. It is validated by composite sampling at a handful of plants. It outputs load by active ingredient by plant, mapped to marketing-authorization-holder market shares for an allocation formula. A 'source-control screen' flags plants where pretreatment at a large care home or hospital removes more load per euro than plant-scale ozone or activated carbon, as a candidate for levy credits. The methodology is published so the scheme operator can defend it.
why_now: The directive is in transposition and the scheme design is being fought over now. The 10x cost disagreement means both utilities and producers need defensible numbers before 2028. European aging keeps raising per-capita medication load.
revenue_model: Per-study fees of EUR 25-80k for water boards. Annual licenses of EUR 100-250k to national scheme operators and industry associations for the allocation engine and yearly re-runs. Later, consulting on care-home source-control projects.
non_obvious_insight: The cost fight will be won by whoever supplies a referee-grade attribution dataset. The best predictor of load is not at the pipe but at the pillbox: age-structured dispensing and care-home density explain most of it. Demographics is the missing variable in water-quality economics, and neither water engineers nor pharma-market analysts hold both halves.
first_30_days: Start with the Netherlands and Germany, where open national dispensing statistics exist (for example the Dutch GIP databank). Model 5 mid-size catchments. Cold-pitch two regional water boards and one pharma producer association with the one-page result. Aim to close paid pilots at EUR 15-25k.

title: Distributor Credit Radar for Failing Restaurants
one_liner: A weekly early-warning score on each restaurant account, built from public signals and distributors' own order and payment data, so food distributors can tighten terms before the customer goes dark.
customer: Independent foodservice distributors (produce, protein, dairy, beverage, paper) with $20-500M in revenue that sell on net-14 and net-30 terms to restaurants. The buyer is the credit manager, controller or owner.
problem: Restaurants are high-turnover, thinly capitalized credit risks, and distributors are unsecured creditors who see the problem last. Generic credit bureaus are weak on restaurants. When consumer spending is squeezed and rates are higher, bad debt climbs and distributors respond with blunt tools (COD for everyone) that lose good accounts.
solution: A risk score per account, refreshed weekly, combining health-inspection trends, permit and liquor-license status, lien and judgment filings, review and hours changes, delivery-platform activity, foot traffic, and the distributor's own signals (order-size decline, days-to-pay drift). Alerts recommend cutting limits, switching to COD or accelerating collection. A consortium data pool of anonymized payment experience improves the score for every member. A bad-debt shield insurance product can follow.
why_now: Squeezed lower-income consumers, higher borrowing costs and the energy-cost shock raise restaurant failures. Public and alternative data on restaurants is now cheap to assemble, and distributors are digitizing accounts receivable and order data.
revenue_model: $600-2,500 per month per distributor by account count, plus consortium data access and later an insurance referral share.
non_obvious_insight: Restaurants fail visibly weeks or months before they stop paying. The best predictor is the distributor's own order-size decline, which they are not analyzing, and the consortium effect (shared payment behavior) becomes a data moat no single distributor can build.
first_30_days: Get three regional distributors to share two years of anonymized accounts-receivable history and back-test whether public signals warn 8-12 weeks before write-offs. Sell a paid pilot at $1,500 per month. Each avoided $20k write-off pays for the subscription for a year.

title: Shelf Zero: Unclaimed Cremains Clearance Service
one_liner: A done-for-you compliance service that legally and respectfully empties the closet of unclaimed ashes that nearly every funeral home and crematory is afraid to touch.
customer: Independent funeral homes and crematories, where the owner or office manager pays per container. Secondary buyers are county public administrators and medical examiner offices. A third group is owners preparing to sell, whose buyers will flag the shelf in diligence.
problem: Cremation is now the majority disposition and still climbing. Families ghost after the cremation: an unpaid balance, an estrangement, a move, or a death of the only relative. State law on unclaimed remains varies widely. Search results show, for example, 120 days after written notice in Minnesota, at least 121 days in Texas, 60 days in Ohio and Nebraska, and 90 days with cemetery-contract rules in California. Directors won't scatter anything without a bulletproof paper trail, because one angry cousin surfacing four years later is a lawsuit or a board complaint. So the boxes pile up. A two-generation-old home can have dozens or hundreds, and staff feel guilt every time they walk past the shelf.
solution: A per-state playbook run as a service. Intake is a spreadsheet upload of name, date, contract and contact. Then skip-tracing for next of kin and authorizing agents, certified-mail and email notices on the statutory timeline, and a timestamped evidence file. Lawful disposition follows, through partner columbarium common niches, scattering gardens or sea scattering, each with a signed Certificate of Lawful Disposition per box. Veterans are identified through records requests and routed to the free national-cemetery inurnment route and Missing in America Project-type volunteers. Families who surface late can still reclaim through the funeral home for a small fee. An ongoing alert that flags containers at day 30, 60 and 90 stops the shelf refilling.
why_now: Cremation share keeps rising and household budgets are stretched, so abandonment is increasing. Consolidators such as SCI keep buying independents (about 22 funeral homes and 2 cemeteries for roughly $101M in 2025 per its filings). Their diligence treats an uncleared shelf as a liability, so retiring third-generation owners suddenly need a clean inventory. Skip-tracing and document automation are now cheap enough to run per box at a profit.
revenue_model: $175-$400 per container, tiered by state notice complexity. A $1,500-$3,000 pre-sale shelf audit and clearance bundle sells to owners about to list. A $49-$99/month ongoing aging-alert subscription covers new cases. Disposition partner fees (niche, scattering, transport) are passed through with a margin.
non_obvious_insight: The problem isn't the ashes, it's the paper trail. Nobody wants to be the person who scattered too early, so the shelf grows for decades. Outsiders assume it's a handful of boxes and a sad footnote. Inside, it's a compounding legal and emotional liability that every owner would pay a flat fee to make disappear, and the product being sold is really indemnifying documentation plus dignity, not disposal logistics.
first_30_days: Pick Ohio, Minnesota and Texas, where statutory safe harbors are clearest. Pay a funeral-law attorney a few thousand dollars to draft the three state notice templates and the disposition certificate. Offer a free 'shelf audit' to 30 homes via the state funeral directors' association newsletter and the private director Facebook groups. Convert five homes at $250 per box as pilots. Sign one local columbarium or church for a common-niche arrangement and one veterans-remains volunteer chapter.

title: AI-Aware E&O Cover for Solo Consultants
one_liner: A specialty insurance agency for laid-off professionals turned solo consultants whose errors-and-omissions cover may quietly exclude AI-assisted work, with premiums discounted for logged verification workflows.
customer: Solo and 2-10-person consultancies (fractional CFOs, marketing and analytics freelancers, dev contractors, HR and ops consultants) pay $400-1,500 a year in premium. The agency earns roughly 15-20% commission.
problem: Large carriers have reportedly sought AI-liability exclusions, so a freelancer who used AI on a deliverable can find a claim denied. Client contracts increasingly demand E&O plus AI-use reps. Newly independent laid-off professionals never read the policy language.
solution: A retail agency that places policies with carriers offering affirmative AI coverage (an MGA program later). A lightweight verification log (source checks, review sign-off) yields an underwriting-friendly attestation that lowers price. A contract clause checker flags indemnities, plus a template AI-use disclosure for clients.
why_now: Carrier AI-exclusion filings surfaced in late 2025, layoffs are creating a wave of new independents, and enterprise procurement now asks vendors for AI-use attestations. AI-liability startups target enterprises, not solos.
revenue_model: Commissions of 15-20%, MGA fees later, and a $10-a-month verification-log tool.
non_obvious_insight: The gap is one of underwriting information: how AI-assisted work is actually verified versus what the policy assumes. A logged verification workflow is data an insurer will pay for with lower prices. Premiums are too small for big brokers to chase, so a new insured class goes unserved.
first_30_days: Partner with a licensed E&O producer (or get licensed). Read the AI language of 10 carriers and publish a 'Does your E&O cover AI?' checker and newsletter for laid-off and freelancer communities. Bind the first 20 policies.

title: Medicaid Look-Back Packet Builder
one_liner: Turn 60 months of messy bank statements into a caseworker-ready Medicaid application packet with explanations, so families avoid 'failure to provide verification' denials.
customer: Adult children and POA agents applying for nursing-home Medicaid for a parent ($299-$499 per case), plus elder-law and Medicaid-planning firms and senior placement advisors ($500-$1,500/month seats or per-case fees).
problem: Long-term-care Medicaid reviews up to 60 months of statements for every open account and every account closed within the window. Caseworkers typically demand written explanations for each expenditure over about $500. If records are missing the application is likely denied for 'failure to provide verification'. POA agents often lack online access to old or closed accounts, and banks can charge research fees for paper copies. Meanwhile the parent's care bills accumulate and elder-law attorneys charge thousands.
solution: Upload statements (PDF, CSV or bank link) and use OCR and an LLM to build the ledger. Detect large transfers, gifts, transfers to relatives and round-number withdrawals. Show likely penalty-period exposure. Draft the explanation letters and a caseworker index with state-specific checklists. Auto-generate missing-statement request letters to banks with a POA cover page, track which accounts are still missing, and hand the attorney a clean exception report. A separate 'consolidate and simplify before you need Medicaid' mode targets families planning ahead.
why_now: Document extraction and bank-data aggregation now make a 60-month review a minutes-long task rather than paralegal hours. Federal law (H.R. 1) sets a $1M Medicaid home-equity cap from Jan 1, 2028, and the 2026 baseline is $752,000 in most states, so more middle-class families in expensive housing markets will need spend-down or planning. State caseworkers will also be stretched by the 2027 work-requirement rollout, making complete first-time packets more valuable.
revenue_model: $299-$499 per family packet, $99 'look-back risk scan' as a lead magnet, and $500-$1,500/month firm seats or $75-$150 per case for elder-law offices, with placement-advisor referral fees as a secondary channel.
non_obvious_insight: The denial reason is paperwork, not eligibility: the requirement to explain each $500+ transaction and produce statements for closed accounts is a software-shaped burden that elder-law attorneys currently bill by the hour. See the documentation rules and 'likely deny for failure to provide verification' language at https://www.paelderlaw.net/medicaid-application-process-5-year-look-back-5-years-of-records-for-small-and-inactive-accounts/. The home-equity change is at https://justiceinaging.org/hr1-imposes-new-limit-on-home-equity-for-medicaid-ltss-effective-2028/. Bank refusal to deal with POA agents compounds it (https://www.aarp.org/caregiving/financial-legal/power-of-attorney-bank-approval/). Reddit was unreachable, so this rests on legal-practice and AARP sources describing the recurring r/AgingParents 'Mom needs Medicaid, what do they want?' situation.
first_30_days: Start with one state with clear caseworker checklists (Pennsylvania or New York). Hand-build 5 packets for free for local elder-law paralegals to validate the exception logic, then productize statement parsing and letter generation. Sell a $99 risk scan and a $349 packet through caregiver Facebook groups and 3-5 elder-law and placement-advisor partners, aiming for 10 paid packets and one firm pilot.

title: Gate-Risk Radar for Evergreen Private Credit
one_liner: A quarterly shadow NAV and gate-probability score for every non-traded BDC and interval fund, sold to the RIAs and OCIOs who put clients into them.
customer: Independent RIAs and family offices ($100M to $3B AUM) with client money in non-traded BDCs, interval and tender-offer funds, at $400 to $1,500 per month per firm. Secondary buyers are TAMPs and wealth platforms (API license) and 401(k) advisers as alternatives enter defined-contribution plans.
problem: Advisers learn a fund has gated from a sponsor letter after the tender window closes. In Q1 2026 non-traded BDC investors requested about $13.9B and got about $7.4B. Blackstone gated BCRED in June 2026 with about 5% fills, and Q2 requests hit a record 12.4% of NAV with only 38% filled. Reported NAVs are smoothed, and nobody tells an adviser whether the next tender will be pro-rated or what to file.
solution: Ingest the tender-offer filings (window and cap), 10-Q and N-PORT marks, non-accruals and PIK share, listed-BDC discount to NAV, secondary bids on non-traded shares, and loan-index prices. Output three things per fund: (1) shadow NAV against reported NAV, (2) probability that the next tender gates and the expected fill rate, (3) a 'if I request X, expect to receive Y' calculator. Add compliance-ready client letters. Start as a public tracker of about 40 funds, then put the alerts and calculator behind a paywall.
why_now: 2026 is the first year pro-rata gating hit the whole non-traded BDC category. Blue Owl merged a non-traded BDC into its listed sibling under redemption pressure. The August 2025 executive order opening 401(k)s to alternatives is about to push far more retail money into these wrappers. Private-credit blowups in late 2025 turned advisers from curious to scared.
revenue_model: Tiered subscription for advisers, an enterprise API for wealth platforms and TAMPs, and a $250 per-fund 'client-ready due diligence memo' for compliance files.
non_obvious_insight: Pro-rata gating makes over-requesting the dominant strategy. Once investors expect a 14 to 38 cent fill, they file bigger requests than they need, so request size becomes a self-amplifying signal. It overstates true demand but predicts fill rates well. The gap between the listed-BDC discount and reported NAV leads request size by about a quarter. Quants see this as a bank-run game with strategic complements, not a credit-loss story, and nobody in wealth tech models it that way.
first_30_days: Scrape EDGAR tender-offer, 10-Q and N-PORT filings for about 40 funds and publish a free weekly 'gate watch' on LinkedIn and Substack framed as research. DM 100 RIA compliance heads and CIOs. Convert 10 to a $500-per-month pilot and start talks with two wealth-platform data teams.

title: Voice-Clone-Proof Verbal Deals for Grain and Cattle
one_liner: A two-channel confirmation step and verified-payee ledger that makes phone-and-handshake commodity deals safe from cloned voices and redirected payments.
customer: Regional grain elevators and co-ops, livestock auction markets and order buyers, ag input retailers, and the ag lenders that finance them.
problem: Agriculture runs on calls: bids, forward contracts, cattle sales, input prepays and cash rents, with confirmation by email. About 3 seconds of audio can clone a farmer's or merchandiser's voice, and BEC cost $3.05B in 2025. Retail beef hit a record $9.64/lb, contract sizes are up, and farm distress attracts fake-buyer scams. Small operations have no fraud team, and cross-bank recovery through the FBI's process is rarely accessible to them.
solution: Verify each farmer's bank account ownership once, with a passphrase or app approval. Any verbal contract above a threshold, or any change of payee, triggers an out-of-band push approval or a callback to a pre-registered number. Settlement pays only to verified accounts. Integrate with grain accounting and auction-clerk systems. Extend to cash-rent payments to older landlords and to the December input prepay season.
why_now: Voice cloning is mainstream. Chainalysis reports impersonation scams up 1,400% with average payments up 253%, and the FBI's Sept 17 2026 PSA cites AI video calls in law-enforcement impersonation. The December prepay season is about ten weeks away, and record livestock prices raise the stakes.
revenue_model: $300-800 a month per elevator or auction location plus $0.50-2 per verified payment. Lenders pay per portfolio, and cyber insurers may give premium credits.
non_obvious_insight: In agriculture the voice is the credential. Forty-year relationships mean nobody asks for ID, and voice cloning breaks the oldest trust protocol in commodity trading. The paying customer is the elevator or auction, which bears misdirected settlements, not the farmer. The tool plugs into settlement systems that banks cannot see.
first_30_days: Interview 20 elevator merchandisers and controllers. Pilot with 2 regional co-ops during harvest settlements using a bank account-owner check plus text push approval. Present to auction-market clerk groups. Ask a cyber-insurance broker about premium credits. Offer a December prepay fraud drill.

title: Fractional Licensed Qualifier for Trade-Business Buyers
one_liner: Rent a vetted master-licensed professional as the bona fide qualifying officer, so first-time buyers of HVAC, plumbing, electrical and engineering firms can get financed and keep the license alive after the seller leaves.
customer: First-time acquirers (search funders, SBA-financed individual buyers, independent sponsors, small holdcos) of licensed-trade companies with $1-15M revenue. The buyer pays monthly. SBA lenders and business brokers are the referral channel.
problem: In licensed trades the license and credentials are the real asset, and they walk out the door with the seller at closing. Buyers without a license get rejected by banks, and a replacement certification takes 6-12 months. Search-fund and ETA (entrepreneurship through acquisition) volume is at record levels, so more non-credentialed buyers are chasing these businesses.
solution: A bench of retired or semi-retired license holders (master plumbers, electrical contractors, PEs, inspectors, HVAC qualifiers). Each is placed as a bona fide officer or employee under a state-specific structure with real supervisory duties, E&O cover and indemnity. The service comes with (1) a lender-ready 'credential continuity package' (letter, duties, key-person plan), (2) a 12-month program that sponsors an internal successor through exams and hours, and (3) a state-by-state compliance library. It operates only in states where counsel confirms the qualifier rules allow this. License-lending schemes are illegal in many states, so compliance is the moat.
why_now: About 100 new US/Canadian search funds launched in 2023 (record), and acquisition volume grew from $110M to $880M per Stanford data summarized on Wikipedia. More than half of US small-business owners are 55+ without succession plans. PE Hub's September 2026 feed shows continuing PE appetite for HVAC, pest control and vet add-ons, which lifts what owners of licensed businesses expect to be paid and pulls more of them into sale processes. Buyer supply now exceeds credentialed-buyer supply.
revenue_model: $2-4K/month retainer per placement for 12-24 months. $1.5-2.5K one-time lender package. Sponsored successor-certification program billed at cost plus margin. Later, group E&O and key-person insurance placement commissions.
non_obvious_insight: The binding constraint in trades acquisitions is the credential, not capital or price. Jack Rauch's Tew & Taylor deal was rejected by multiple banks because he had no building-code license or experience. Their words: 'you don't have this license, you don't have this experience... good luck. We won't touch it.' He had to close on family-office debt at a 33/33/33 cap table (https://www.acquiringminds.co/articles/jack-rauch-tew-taylor). Manolo Diaz Corrada's Bonneville deal names certifications as a single point of failure that take 'six months to a year to acquire' and are not economical to duplicate (https://www.acquiringminds.co/articles/manolo-diaz-corrada-bonneville-group). Nobody sells credential continuity as a product. Brokers treat it as the buyer's problem, and lenders treat it as a deal-killer. Caveat: the evidence is operator interviews with a small sample, and the legal structure must be validated state by state.
first_30_days: Pick two states with well-documented qualifier rules (for example FL and TX) and pay for a counsel memo on each. Recruit 10 retired license holders through trade associations, retiree groups and union alumni networks. Build a one-page lender-facing continuity plan and show it to 10-15 SBA lenders and 20 business brokers. Post the offer in ETA communities (Searchfunder, Acquiring Minds audience) and sign 2-3 buyers with signed LOIs for paid pilot placements at a discount in exchange for case studies.

title: Immune-Training Forest-Floor Yards for Daycares
one_liner: A certified installation and refill service that replaces sterile daycare yards with vetted forest floor and sod to diversify children's skin and gut microbiota.
customer: Private daycare chains, preschool operators, nature-based preschools and municipal early-childhood departments in cities, especially ones competing on parent trust and outdoor programming.
problem: Allergies, asthma and immune disorders are rising in urban kids, who spend 8+ hours a day in daycare yards of plastic, gravel and rubber mulch with almost no microbial diversity. Parents worry, but the options are vague 'nature play' features with no evidence of health impact.
solution: Biodiversity kits based on the Finnish protocol: about 100 m2 of pathogen-screened forest floor litter and 200 m2 of sod, planter boxes and simple play rules, sourced from vetted local woodland. We add a seasonal refill and an optional microbiome swab study, all under a 'Biodiversity Certified' badge that daycares can show to parents.
why_now: There is direct peer-reviewed evidence. In a study of 10 Finnish daycares with 75 children aged 3-5, adding forest floor and sod for 28 days changed skin and gut microbiota and immune markers (Roslund et al., Science Advances, 2020), and a 2021 follow-up on long-term effects was published. Parents are more microbiome-aware, and cities are funding cooling and greening of schoolyards.
revenue_model: One-time install of roughly $6-15k per yard plus an annual refill subscription of roughly $1-2k per year, since the biology decays and litter needs replacing. Licensing of the certification badge to chains, and public-tender revenue from cities.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody can patent dirt, so the moat is safe sourcing, pathogen testing and certification, and the recurring consumable makes it a regional supply chain of local ecological material. Selling 'immune infrastructure' to childcare works because the buyer's real problem is parent trust, and a visible, evidence-backed feature beats a marketing claim.
first_30_days: Contact 10 forest schools and one small chain. Build a 30 m2 pilot with a local soil scientist and a university microbiologist for about $1.5k. Set up a baseline and follow-up swab pilot and sell the first three paid yards to chains that want a differentiator.

title: Biotech Graveyard Data Exchange
one_liner: Rescue, clean and license the wet-lab data of shutting-down biotechs, especially the failed and negative results that AI drug-discovery models are starved of, and split the proceeds with the estate.
customer: AI-drug-discovery companies, big-pharma computational groups and ML-for-bio labs that license proprietary training data (ADME/tox, assay panels, SAR series, structural data). The sellers are wind-down estates, VCs and founders, who get a revenue share instead of paying anything.
problem: After the 2022-2025 biotech funding drought, hundreds of venture-backed biotechs have shut down or been hollowed out. When the last employee leaves, years of proprietary experimental data die on unpaid cloud accounts, expired ELN and LIMS licenses and laptops. Meanwhile AI models are trained on published literature, which is survivorship-biased: negative results almost never get published. Models lack the data on what does not work, and that data is exactly what dead companies hold.
solution: A wind-down data-salvage service, done in a 60-day window between the last payroll and server deletion. Triage what data exists and what is encumbered (licensor and CRO rights, academic-license terms). Extract from ELN, LIMS, instruments and cloud buckets. Limit the first scope to non-human-subject data such as biochemical and cell assays, chemistry, DMPK and structural data, so there is no PII problem. Get IP and rights sign-off from the estate or assignee. Standardize to a common assay schema with provenance. License as curated bundles to AI-bio and pharma buyers, with revenue flowing back to the estate.
why_now: The biotech shutdown and reverse-merger wave is in full swing, with wind-down specialists and startup shutdown services now established. AI-bio companies and pharma are openly competing for proprietary data, including federated and data-for-model-access programs. The 23andMe data-in-bankruptcy episode showed how badly data is currently handled in wind-downs. Cheap LLM-assisted schema mapping now makes normalizing messy legacy assay data affordable.
revenue_model: Free or low-cost triage for the estate. Take 30-50% of licensing revenue on each bundle, plus a fixed curation fee charged to buyers. Later, sell subscription access to a growing pooled 'negative results' corpus organized by target class.
non_obvious_insight: The dataset with the most scarcity value is the one everyone considers worthless: failed programs. Sellers are motivated because the alternative is deletion, and there is no consumer-privacy problem in assay data, unlike almost every other 'data for AI' market. The moat is trust and presence at the exact moment a company dies, meaning relationships with wind-down lawyers, biotech VCs and CFO-for-hire networks, not technology.
first_30_days: Reach out to 20 biotech VC platform partners, wind-down lawyers and fractional CFOs with a one-page offer of free data triage, revenue share and zero cost to the estate. Sign 2-3 shutting-down biotechs. Pre-sell sample packs to 3-5 AI-bio buyers and get a letter of intent on price per curated dataset. Build the minimal schema-normalization pipeline on the first dataset and get legal templates for estate-to-exchange licensing. Ship the first licensed bundle within the first 2-3 months.

title: Secret-Shopper Audits of Government Algorithms
one_liner: Submit synthetic applicants and questions to public benefits systems, chatbots and eligibility tools to measure real error and denial rates, then sell the evidence.
customer: State auditors and legislative oversight offices, legal-aid funders, civil-rights litigators, and government AI vendors that want an independent seal before a contract renewal.
problem: State and local buyers cannot audit the AI they bought, and no one owns post-award monitoring. Michigan's fraud detector wrongly accused 40,000 people and cost $20M plus $78M for a replacement. Contracts run 7 years with only 3% of provisions covering cybersecurity.
solution: Run agent-driven synthetic-case testers against public-facing eligibility screeners, 311 and permit chatbots, and (with authorization) internal decision tools. Publish error-rate and disparity reports with reproducible test cases. Offer a continuous monitoring subscription to buyers.
why_now: Cities and counties have moved from pilots to production AI, and the Glass/Sourcewell marketplace pilot covers about 120 agencies. Agentic testers are cheap in 2026, and Michigan makes the harm undeniable.
revenue_model: $30-120K per audit engagement, $5-15K per month for monitoring, and grant-funded public-interest audits. Vendors pay for certified re-tests.
non_obvious_insight: Public-interest audit funders and state auditors already have budgets and mandate but no measurement tool. The synthetic-case method needs no vendor cooperation and no data access.
first_30_days: Run a free audit of 10 public-facing city or state chatbots and publish the findings. Send the report to state auditors and legal-aid funders. Sign one paid audit from a funder or auditor.
